dialogs.title: حَكِي — بِالْعِيَادَة
dialogs.intro: Budi has had a fever for two days and goes to the clinic near his home.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: I have a headache and a fever.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.baca: min yōmēn. w hal’i waaji‘ni kamaan.
lines.id: For two days. My throat hurts too.
lines.literal: from two-days. and throat-my hurting-me also.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.baca: shway. w ma fiini aakul mniih.
lines.id: A little. And I can't eat properly.
lines.literal: a-little. and not can-I I-eat well.

lines.speaker: اَلدُّكْتُور:
lines.id: Let me have a look. Open your mouth.

lines.speaker: اَلدُّكْتُور:
lines.text: لَا، اِلْتِهَاب بَسِيط. مَا فِي دَاعِي تِخَاف.
lines.baca: la’, iltihaab basiiṭ. ma fi daa‘i tikhaaf.
lines.id: No, a mild infection. Nothing to worry about.
lines.literal: no, inflammation simple. not there-is reason you-fear.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Thank God. What should I take?

lines.speaker: اَلدُّكْتُور:
lines.text: رَح إِكْتِبْلَك دَوَا. حَبِّة تْلَات مَرَّات بِالْيَوْم.
lines.baca: rah iktiblak dawa. habbe tlaat marraat bil-yōm.
lines.id: I'll write you a prescription. One pill three times a day.
lines.literal: will I-write-for-you medicine. pill three times in-the-day.

lines.speaker: اَلدُّكْتُور:
lines.text: خَمْس تْيَام. وْاِشْرَب مَي كْتِير وْاِرْتَاح.
lines.baca: khams tyaam. w ishrab mayy ktiir w irtaah.
lines.id: Five days. And drink lots of water and rest.
lines.literal: five days. and drink water much and rest.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Thank you, doctor. How much is it?

notes: **⚠️ The part that hurts is the subject, not you.** Instead of "I have a headache," Levantine Arabic says رَاسِي بِوجَعْنِي — literally "my head is hurting me," with the head as the **subject** and you as the **object**. The word order feels very strange at first, then becomes second nature.

**The form وَاجِعْنِي is the active participle, and it's used more than the verb.** رَاسِي وَاجِعْنِي ("my head hurts") is more common than رَاسِي بِوجَعْنِي. For a feminine body part, the form is وَاجْعِتْنِي — for example إِيدِي وَاجْعِتْنِي.
**The word سُخُونِة means fever**, and it comes from سُخْن (heat), which you met in unit 5. You say it with عِنْد — for example عِنْدِي سُخُونِة ("I have a fever"), the same pattern as عِنْدِي وَقْت.
**The phrase سَلَامْتَك is a must-say to anyone who's ill.** Literally "your safety," it means "get well soon." The reply: اَللَّه يْسَلِّمَك. To a woman: سَلَامْتِك.

**The phrase مَا فِي دَاعِي means "there's no need."** It's used to reassure and to decline gently: مَا فِي دَاعِي تِتْعَب حَالَك ("don't go to any trouble"). One of the most useful phrases for the hosting and visiting in unit 20.

**Health care in the Levant often starts at the pharmacy, not the doctor.** Pharmacists in Syria, Lebanon, and Jordan routinely give advice for minor complaints and sell many medicines without a prescription. For a cold or a headache, going straight to the pharmacy is perfectly normal.

grammars.title: Saying what hurts
after: Notice that the participle changes with the body part: وَاجِعْنِي for masculine ones (رَاس، بَطِن، ضَهِر), وَاجْعِتْنِي for feminine ones (إِيد، رِجِل), and وَاجْعِينِي for plurals (سْنَان، عْيُون).
To ask someone else: شُو وَاجْعَك؟ ("what hurts?") or وَين عَم بِوجَعَك؟ ("where does it hurt?"). The answer just names the body part.

grammars.title: Parts of the body
after: The word قَلِب means the heart as an organ and also the "heart" of feelings, just as in English. The phrase عَ قَلْبَك you used in unit 7 comes from it.
Paired body parts (eyes, hands, legs, ears) take the dual form from unit 5: عَيْنَين، إِيدَين، رِجْلَين. These forms are very common and worth memorizing.

blocks.text: The phrase حَاسِس حَالِي مِش مْنِيح is the most common way to say "I don't feel well" without going into detail. The feminine form is حَاسْسِة حَالِي مِش مْنِيحَة. It's enough to start a conversation with any pharmacist.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Allergies: sentences to learn by heart
items: The pattern: عِنْدِي حَسَاسِيِّة مِن… — for example عِنْدِي حَسَاسِيِّة مِن الْبِنِسِلِين.
For food: مَا بَاكُل… لَإِنّ عِنْدِي حَسَاسِيِّة ("I don't eat… because I'm allergic").
In an emergency, one word always works: إِسْعَاف *is‘aaf* (ambulance). Emergency numbers differ from country to country — look yours up on your first day, don't wait.

blocks.text: The word حَبِّة, which meant "a piece of fruit" in unit 6, here means "a pill" — same word, same counting unit, different context. For syrup, use شَرَاب; for an injection, إِبْرَة.

blocks.title: What to say to someone who's ill, and the replies
items: To someone who's ill: **سَلَامْتَك** *salaamtak*. The reply: **اَللَّه يْسَلِّمَك**.
To someone who's just recovered: **اَلْحَمْدُ لِلَّه عَ السَّلَامِة** *alhamdulilla ‘a es-salaame*.
A deeper wish for someone seriously ill: **اَللَّه يِشْفِيك** *alla yishfiik* ("may God heal you").
I've had a fever for two days.
Do you have anything for a headache?
